narrative_purpose: Makes sterilising regeneration more frightening than felling a mature tree: an apparently intact forest can already be doomed if its seed bank, woodsprites, and living soil have been erased.
subject: A matched two-part forest-floor study beneath equally large mature trees. Left: the soil is dense with dormant seeds, fine fungal threads, tiny roots, and several translucent woodsprites settling onto moist ground; small seedlings of different species are emerging. Right: the adult trunks still stand above, but the soil beneath is pale, compacted, and chemically scorched, with empty seed husks, dead fungal threads, no woodsprites, and no seedlings anywhere; the canopy looks alive while the ground holds no next generation.
scene: Two futures hidden under similar standing forests: one with a distributed recovery reserve and one already reproductively dead.
camera: Side-on soil cutaway at ground level, matching canopy roots and soil depth across both halves.
light: Living soil glows softly in cyan and teal; sterile soil is dim stone-grey with one faint sickly amber trace and no internal glow.
palette: Cool living colours on the fertile side, desaturated stone and near-black on the sterile side, warm contamination kept scarce.
style: Painterly ecological naturalist cutaway with close soil detail.
detail_level: Fine seeds, hyphae, and seedlings on the living side; stark empty texture and broken remnants on the sterile side.
composition: Equal underground panels, mature trunks cropped similarly above, strong negative space in the sterile soil for later callouts.
consistency_notes: The adult forest on both sides should look initially similar; the decisive contrast is belowground capacity for future recovery.
negative_prompt: no text, no labels, no arrows, no people, no laboratory glassware, no photographic or 3D-render look, no bright orange contamination
